utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said we would be dealing with the documents yesterday. Now we received the list from Miletic Defence, the list of the documents they mean to tender. Do you have any objections, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We have no objections to the Miletic list nor to the other lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is any other Defence team minded to say anything? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was asking other Defence about your documents. Okay. We have also received the list from the Prosecution. I take it that you have no objection. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've a couple of observations come clarification issues, Your Honours. First of all in relation to 2669B. There was some confusion Your Honour will recall about this two days ago at 29108. I could go through the history of this document, but I will try and cut this extremely short. It was originally on a list to be put to General Milovanovic both in the A and the B form, but it was not actually put to him. That can be confirmed by the transcript at 12396 on the 1st of June of last year. Mr. Butler was asked about one particular version of the document. It's not entirely clear to us which version he was asked about. The translation that was put to him is clearly a different translation, the one that we now have. To be fair to the Prosecution, I suspect that that translation was a draft translation. I say that having looked at the transcript. The English is less good than it is now in the hard copy that I have in front of me. That was on the 16th of January of this year at 19764. Thereafter, as far as we can make out, the document was tendered as A. And then as we know, the document -- one of the versions was put to General Masal. I'm not too sure which. Mr. Thayer may be able to help as far as that is concerned. But as far as we can make out, the only translation that exists is in relation to A, not B. That's certainly the ERN of the English translation on the list that I have in front of me relates to 2669A, not B. They're the same document, by the way, but there are different annotations, handwritten annotations on them. So I'm unclear as to why the Prosecution is seeking to admit a second version of this document, whether there's any significance in the two different version, clarification of which was put to Mr. Butler, which was put to General Masal, which we have the translation of; and, frankly, a last whinge if I may why wasn't this put to General Milovanovic who was the author of the document? Why was it got in through the back door through these other people, but that's a different point for a different day perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer, if you could clarify this issue. Do you need some time to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it might be a better use of the Trial Chamber's time if I did take a couple of minutes back at my desk and see if there's anything really to this, and I'll report back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I forgot to mention that Miletic documents will be admitted in their entirety, and then the Prosecution documents will be admitted except for -- oh, yes. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Would I like to make an observation concerning the last six documents on the Prosecution exhibits list which are directly related to a motion which has been filed by three of the Defence team concerning the use of documents not in evidence and not on the Prosecution Rule 65 ter list. Therefore, we do not object to those documents being admitted on the record but subject, of course, to those -- that pending motion. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Prosecution documents will be admitted except for the one, number of which is 2669B, which will be marked for identification for the time being, and the others will be admitted with the caveat that we note the observation of Mr. Bourgon. So that's without prejudice to our decision, which will be forthcoming with respect to the motion pending. And we also have a document from Gvero team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. That's why I was on my feet. It's 6DP3905.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Is there any objection from any parties? Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's admitted as well. Shall we bring in the witness, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Babic. We will proceed with your evidence today. Yesterday you spoke about the 67th Communications Regiment. In addition to the 67th Regiment, in the establishment structure of the Main Staff was there any other organ that dealt with communications?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska there was the communications organ that consisted of its chief and a desk officer. The chief was the chief of communications, Colonel Prole, Radomir Prole, and the desk officer in the communications organ for encryption was Lieutenant Colonel Milisav Radakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What was the role of that organ, please?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the communications organ was to plan all necessary communications for command and control for informing and reporting for airspace surveillance and reporting to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the unit in which you were the Chief of Staff, which was the 67th Regiment, did it submit combat reports, and if it did, who did it submit to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We submitted regular reports when the war started. And sometime up to mid-1993, we submit written reports, and as of that time onwards the reports were oral. We submitted reports to the deputy chief of the Main Staff at first to the chief of the Main Staff, and later on to the operations department in the operations centre where General Miletic was at the time. At that time, he was colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify one thing. In the initial period of time who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our written reports were submitted -- or, rather, brought directly to the operations centre, and later on it was ordered for these reports to be submitted orally; and we all reported orally to the Chief of Staff, and after that the Chief of Staff ordered us to report directly to the operations centre where General Miletic was and spent most of his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have one clarification? When he first answered that the translation I got was that the oral report went to the deputy chief of the Main Staff, then the chief of the Main Staff, and then to the operations department; and I don't know if that's what that is or that's a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you heard the comments of Mr. McCloskey. Could you clarify your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we are talking about a long period of time over the year 1993, obviously there were some changes in the way we submitted our reports. In the initial period, we submitted written reports. That was our common practice. And since the unit was in contact with the Main Staff, i.e., shared the same area of some 100 metres, the regiment command was at a hundred -- a hundred metres distance, it was regulated after that not to issue written reports but, rather, to submit them orally. At first the situation in the unit was more or less well known. The chief of the Main Staff ordered us to convey our oral reports directly to the operations centre. I'm talking about the year 1993 when things started. The following year, in 1994, the reports were submit orally in the operations centre, and this is where General Miletic spent most of his time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you first reported to the chief of Main Staff, and later you reported to the operations centre orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And just one more question, please. Who was the chief of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska throughout all that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout all that time the chief of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska was General Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, what types of communications means were used in the Main Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of communications issued a plan of communications which encompassed radio relay communications, wire connections, telephone lines, coded teleprinter communications. We also used PTT lines, and radio communication was a fallback position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say that radio communication was a fallback position, that it was on stand-by, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that they were up and running. They were checked, and they were checked regularly, but they were not used by the command of the Main Staff for their regular communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Which devices were used in the territory of what we call Veliki Zep?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used radio relay communications means. Those were SMC 1306B. The radio relay device RRU 9B and FM 200. Also, a radio relay device RRU 800, and a radio relay device RRU 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the Court please produce P183.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P183.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, on the screen, which is on your right-hand side, you will shortly see a document. I would kindly ask you to look at it carefully and read it, and then I'll have some questions for you based on that document on the screen. Tell me when you are done reading.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the 14th of July -- or, rather, in mid-July 1995, were you at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this type of device that is mentioned in the document, which is radio device 2/2 K and KZU-63. Was used at the Main Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not establish this type of communication. My regiment did not, but it had on its strength the devices that are mentioned in the document 2/2 K and KZU-63.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In addition to establishing telephone lines, i.e., communication lines in the Main Staff, the 67th Communications Regiment, i.e., the signals branch, was also dealing with the protection of written texts or written communication. You said that. In your organisational establishment, as a unit of the Main Staff together with the signals branch, did you deal with these tasks?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We established a system of communications which provided, to a certain extent, for the protection of spoken information. That protection was provided to the level of the commands of the immediately subordinated units, i.e., corps commands. In addition to the protection of oral confirmation, the regiment also developed a system of protection of written information. The Communications Regiment had a centre with a -- an encryption centre which dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you still have the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From the aspect of encryption and dispatching telegrams, the document that you see in front of you, would that reflect the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document in my view does not reflect the actual situation for several reasons. It is not a fair representation of the situation. The reasons that I'm -- that I have in mind are of technical nature. First of all, it could not have been type on a teleprinter because it is -- the layout is not correct. Second of all, the document is not signed, which means that it was not transmitted through the communications lines that existed in the system of communication -- communications of the Main Staff that were serviced by the Communications Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In order for a document to be dispatched and received properly, is there anything else that this document should contain? Please wait until I finish my question.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every document that is received or dispatched through the technical means of communication has to have a stamp denoting the time when it was received. This is the establishment stamp of the operator that received it, and every document has to be registered at the encryption centre and then in the files of the command. And that's why I'm saying that this document is irregular. Its contents are what they are, but it looks irregular to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce Exhibit P192.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, would you please look at this document. You don't have to go into the substance. Just look at the heading and look at the signature block. Bottom right. As well as the handwritten addition, bottom left, where it says: "Transmitted, 1510, 13 July 1995." Also, would you please, from the viewpoint of your specialisation, tell us whether this communication had been transmitted and received and if there is any proof that it had been received at any of the addresses indicated.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, like the previous one, is not certified by the signature and the stamp of the senior officer who was supposed to have written it judging by the contents. Second, this document could not have been transmitted via means of communications because, again, there is no stamp of the station that had received it, and it had not been registered by that station. It's still probably in the register of the Main Staff. This is written on a typewriter. We did not have typewriters. We had teletypes that produce a different kind of writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, speaking of telegrams, on which side should the signature be?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the document is transmitted by teletype, then the signature of the person who issues the order or approves the document is on the left, always on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We will not be needing this document any more. Mr. Babic, can you tell us about Crna Rijeka? Where was the command located?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the regiment command?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Where was the command of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Main Staff was located in prefab buildings, and the commander of the Main Staff spent most of his time in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat. Did he say "villa"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of the Main Staff, depending on the situation and the level of danger as indicated by threat alerts, would move to the underground part of the installation where there were working premises, and from that underground space would continue in their tasks. The logistics of the Main Staff was in Han Pijesak, in Gora hotel. Next to the logistics command post there was the administration for personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Babic, the interpreters couldn't hear you well. Did you refer to a villa as the place the commander of the Main Staff spent most of his time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We need one more clarification. Speaking, Mr. Babic, of -- perhaps I was not precise enough in my question. When I say "command," I mean the principal command post. Did your answer also refer to the main command post, the basic command post?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The basic command post was in Crna Rijeka, and that's where the command of the Main Staff was. This description that I gave is just that in Han Pijesak there was a logistics command post where the logistics organ was together with the sector for ORMO and personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: These prefab buildings and the underground space, were they connected by a single communications system?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are separated by a distance of 900 metres, and this entire area of Crna Rijeka and the installations within were connected by an underground cable; and it was very simple and easy to adjust the communications system to various requirements. That's why while the command was in the prefab buildings they enjoyed the communications they needed for their work, and in case the danger, when they moved to the underground space, these same communications became available from the underground premises. Everyone had their own offices underground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, please put a pause between the answer and your question. So please wait till the translation is completed. Can I draw your attention to the line 3 of page 12. You started your question, so I couldn't hear that well, but I don't know what it meant, the logistic organ was together with the sector for ORMO and personnel affairs? If you could clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you were talking about the command post. Tell us, please, what organs of the command were housed in that logistics command post?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the logistics command post there was the logistics sector and the sector for organisational mobilisation and personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I believe this is the clarification we need. Tell us, is this the basic command post? In fact, were the basic command post and the logistics command post connected by a single system of communications?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, and they were able to cooperate, first of all, within the command of the Main Staff and down to various units depending on the scope and type of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what type of communication linked these two installations?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Telephone and teletype communications was establish between these two installations through radio relay and wire external routes, and we also use PTT communications. Radio relay external lines included an axis from Veliki Zep to Han Pijesak, and wire communications meant an underground cable linking the barracks in Han Pijesak with installations in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you know if the Main Staff set up forward command posts?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Main Staff set up forward command posts throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the role of the organs of the communications regiment and the communications regiment itself in the setting up of these forward command posts?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to my previous explanation. The regiment was supposed to plan and set up --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure there were many, many forward command posts throughout this war, and I -- procedures change. If we could focus it on the time-frame. I think he's going for the Krajina and the -- and the, you know, 1995, no problem, but the entire war doesn't -- I don't think it help us, and unless he can say it's exactly the same for every IKM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, do you have any comment or -- you can ask generally, or you can concentrate on specific command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was of general nature, and for the time being it was not linked to any particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's my objection. 1992 was very different than 1995, and I don't think that the proper in a general -- is helpful, and its probative value is outweighed by its -- the time and the non-relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, can we hear the situation in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you know whether your unit or communications organ participate in 1994 or 1995 in the establishment of communications at the forward command post of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Communications Regiment was not involved with its equipment, because it did not participate in the setting up of any communications for forward command posts of the Main Staff. However, the chief of communications, Colonel Prole, organised these things through the equipment and resources of communications units which provided communications for the requirements of the corps. In that period, in 1995, the situation in the west, in Drvar, the Communications Regiment provide the equipment and the personnel at the forward command post in Drvar. That means equipment and personnel. It was a smaller number of personnel, people who operated encrypting stations. I don't know of any other involvement of the communications regiment, and I don't think there was any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when such a forward command post is being set up and when communications are organised at this forward command post, are such communications integrated with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends on the situation. In this particular case, as I explained, there were direct communications with the for command post. There was a direct telephone line, and the command line towards the Main Staff. In some other cases it was possible to organise it in a different way, namely that from the forward command post communications be established towards the Main Staff through the corps command, wherein the corps commander would be the intermediary; whereas teletype communications could work in such a way that the corps station would take over documents and work to service the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in 1995 did you used to see General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw General Miletic in 1994 and in 1995 regularly. Not only him, other senior officers as well, almost on a daily basis or several times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How often would you see him in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- the month of July was generally a month where many officers were away on various missions, but I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when you gave us your personal details, you said you were born on the 7th of July, 1950.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where you were on the 7th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of July, 1995, I was in Crna Rijeka, in my unit performing my regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if you saw General Miletic then? Did you have a meeting perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On that day I did not see General Miletic. The circumstances were such that I believe he wasn't even there on that day. It was my birthday. Some of my officers got hang of it and said that I should buy a round of drinks because its my birthday, and people got closer to each other during the war. That's one of the effects of the war, and the smallest excuse was enough for a celebration, and it was my intention that day to invite all the officers who were working in the underground facility, because they sort of hinted that morning they would appreciate that. I thought I would offer them a round of drinks, and we indeed gathered. And since I was on good terms with General Miletic, and since air alerts were very frequent in those days, he spent a lot of time underground, almost all of the time. So I went down to his office and found there a few officers from the Main Staff. I believe there was Colonel Trkulja and this man Micanovic. Dragan Micanovic, who we called Mico, the cartographer, and Major Slobodan Mandic [as interpreted]. I asked after General Miletic, because I wanted to invite him, but I was told that he had gone to Belgrade. I remember that distinctly. And then I believe Mandic came with me because he was together with us in that area where we gathered. We sat down, had a chat. And I remember clearly that General Miletic was not there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just one correction, please. Line 17, line 2, instead of Slobodan Mandic, it should be read Slobodan Mamlic. Mr. Babic, did you say -- or did you mention Major Mamlic as the person present there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned -- I believe I mentioned Slobodan Mamlic, and this is who I had in mind, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At your birthday party were there any other people present?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mostly officers and civilians who enjoyed the status of civilians and officers. The reason for that was different. I don't know whether at that moment they were civilians or officers, but that was that. I said that those were the most experienced and longest-serving personnel. Most of them were at the facility even before the Main Staff arrived. I remember that Goran Bastak was also there. He died soon after the end of the war. Blagoje Obazovic was also there, as well as Zarko Tanasic. Marijan Jerot was one of the people who were there, and some others whom I can't remember at the moment, but there were a dozen or so people, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, for the time being I don't have any more questions for you. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this brings my examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Will there be any cross from any other Defence team? I think it's your turn, Mr. McCloskey, if you can manage without the assistance of Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we'll be getting into too many frequencies and other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic. My name's Peter McCloskey. I represent the Prosecution, and welcome.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've just spoken of, well, the 7th of July, 1995, like it was yesterday. Where was your party in relation to the operations room that General Miletic usually worked?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need a big explanation. Is it in the same building? It was just not clear to me. Or was it some place else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an underground facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My understanding is your party was in the underground facility. We know the OPs room was in the underground facility. Was your party in the OPs room or some place close by?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no. The personnel that was there, I -- the communications centre was always manned. It was in the underground facility. Those were my people, my personnel, and whenever we had a party or a do, we would stage those in the corridor of the underground facility. As you enter the facility and as you pass through the area from which doors lead to the maintenance rooms, there's a corridor and at the very entrance to the corridor there is a wider space, some four metres wide if not more; and there is enough room to sit down, on the one hand, and on the other hand that's how it was regulated. If there was a do in that area we were not a hindrance to anybody. We did not disturb anybody. In the other part there was this communications centre, and in the area where the OPs centre and other offices of the organs of the Main Staff were that was on the other side, and members of the Communications Regiment did not need to go into that area. So what I'm saying is that we held our party at the very entrance into the working part of the facility, in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the operations centre, Miletic's operation centre, have communication equipment in it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the communications lines with OPs centres of the subordinated units ended there, and all the other numbers from the switchboard were transferred into the OPs centre, and there were also lines from the OPs centre into the prefabricated objects and between the OPs centres of various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And who from the 69th was on duty in the OPs centre looking after that equipment?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand your question. You mean who maintained the equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there anybody stationed with that equipment to help the OPs people in communicating? Very simple question.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nobody. Our obligation was to check the status of the communication lines daily, and nobody serviced the communications means in the OPs centre, nobody from the regiment that is. It was the duty of the operations officer who was on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th I believe that it was Colonel Trkulja, Nedeljko Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And office in charge at Crna Rijeka? Who was the top officers in Crna Rijeka that day, the 7th?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who was standing in for the commander of the Main Staff or who was deputising for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the most high-ranking senior officer at Crna Rijeka on July 7th?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Mladic there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think -- it was possible that he was, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Milovanovic there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was not there. Towards the end of 1994 -- or, rather, beginning of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We know all about that, sir. We know he went over to the Krajina. It was a simple question. Just try to answer my question. You can always explain it, but we know that he spent a lot of time in the Krajina then. Okay. How about General Gvero? Was there he on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. General Gvero was somewhere. He was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure General Gvero was somewhere. Where do you think he was?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I did not have any immediate dealings with those officers, so I wouldn't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know who was in charge that day at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. If we're talking about the Communications Regiment, I can tell you, and you're talking to me about the General Staff of which I didn't know much. I didn't have much insight into their dealings, their whereabouts, their movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say Glavni Staff. You didn't have much dealings with the Main Staff I take it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's my point. Do you know what was going on on July 7th, 1995, at Crna Rijeka? Tell us what was going on in the area of -- between Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica and Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on in -- in that area, but I know that immediately before that date, or immediately before those days there was something constantly happening in that area. Something was on all the time. At least that's the kind of information that reached us. The information spoke about military provocations, actions, by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we know there was a war on, so that's not my question. Do you recall the attack on Crna Rijeka itself that month? I think people might have even been killed.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember the Communications Regiment was involved in providing security to the units on its strength and the parts of the Main Staff. An attack was indeed carried out, and two soldiers were killed in the communications regiment and one officer was wounded. That was on the day that I will always remember, and the previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure, that -- that was conducted by Srebrenica or Zepa Muslims, wasn't it, out of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So surely you as the Chief of Staff, the communications officer, knew that on the 6th of July the Drina Corps, including Vinko Pandurevic, who I think you probably should recognise, and his troops had begun the attack on Srebrenica. His troops were in those woods fighting and dying, and you would have known about it on the 7th of July, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you and your fellow officers at the bunker are drinking slivovitz on 7 July. Those guys are in the woods fighting, you don't know anything about it, but you remember who was at your birthday party. Is that what you're testifying to today?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that I didn't know that there was fighting going on. Nobody informed me. I was not informed. And as for our little do, I don't think it was any kind of celebration. There were even more difficult situations. During the war I myself had gone through a number of things, but there was always a way to let the steam, to -- to relax just a little in order to overcome other, bigger problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why didn't you have the party outside, away from Crna Rijeka a little bit, out of the bomb sights, after work?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that was in the evening hours after all daily activities. Second of all, there were very common air attack alerts sounded at the time. And again, this was not a celebration, and I underline that. This was initiated by others, and since I wanted to respect people's will and to support this feeling of camaraderie, I really don't see why this should be considered as something out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we heard about a party that was on the 11th of July that was outside and somewhere around Han Pijesak at somebody's house. Did you get invite to that one?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such party. Could you maybe jog my memory by providing some more details? As far as I can remember, on that day there was no party in Han Pijesak, or at least I can tell you that I did not attend any such party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did your people attend it, anybody from your unit?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know someone from your unit's testified here; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my unit? Yes. There was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Babic. Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a cross-examination, I admit, but there is no foundation for the last question, or at least my learned friend did not lay any foundation to put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he was about to give some reference. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- basically when I say his unit, I mean the 67th unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know someone that testified here from that unit recently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Mr. Babic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know Velo Pajic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Velo Pajic. He was an officer and a platoon commander in charge of UNHF lines, and he spent all the time throughout the war and after the war in the underground facilities of the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you asked me to give you some information to jog your memory. When did you first start to jog your memory about July 7th and your birthday party some 13 years ago?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that period, I continued working for some time, and then I was pensioned off and I started doing other things. At the beginning of 1997, I got a telephone call from Mr. Petrusic. He introduced himself as a member of General Miletic's Defence team. That's when he told me that he wanted to talk to me about the relevant period. I agreed to talk to him. We met in Belgrade, in his office, at the beginning of 19 -- or, rather, 2007. I apologise. I must have misspoken before. I must have said 1997. And then we spoke about the role of the 67th Communications Regiment in providing communications lines. We spoke about his position in the Main Staff, about command, about my relationship with General Miletic and how much I knew him. This is what we discussed in very broad terms. And then he asked me whether I would be willing to testify as a Defence witness for General Miletic and I said yes. And then he said, "Very well. We shall see about that, and we will be in touch." After some time Mr. Petrusic called me again, and that was sometime in March earlier this year, and he asked me whether I would still be willing to testify as I said I would. I repeated that I was willing to testify. He instructed me to prepare documents, and the documents in question would be my passport with a valid visa and a copy of my passport so that the visa could be issued to me. I agreed to that. At the time my passport was about to expire, so I had to renew it. I had to obtain a new passport, which I did. And then the following time he called me was towards the end of September or perhaps the beginning of October, again earlier this year, and we made arrangements to meet so that he could take the documents from me and to discuss some more things. And since I hail from Bosanska Dubica and I reside with my parents and Mr. Petrusic is not familiar with the area, and since I've retired I have been mostly engaged in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- farming, I have an orchard --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Babic. I -- that covers that question. Can you tell me when you first of your three meetings that you describe with the Defence, and that's completely normal, when did you first tell him that you remembered that 13 years ago that General Miletic didn't come to your birthday drinks in the bunker?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the last conversation we had, as I handed over my passport and a copy of it to Mr. Petrusic, he looked at the documents and he spotted my date of birth, I suppose, and then he said, "You were born on the 7th of July, 1950?" And I said, "Yes, I was." And then he asked me, "Do you remember where General Miletic was on the 7th of July, 1995?" I ponder upon the question, and then I realised that I remember, and I shared with him the story that I shared with everybody else today in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long did you ponder before -- before you realised that he wasn't at your drinks?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand you. You're asking me how much time did I need to remember that I had invited people to share a round of drinks with me? I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When Mr. Petrusic pointed out the birthday and asked you about Miletic, how long did it take you before you told him that story that you just told us? I mean, did you remember that day, or did you have to think about it overnight, or did you just respond to him shortly after because it was such a -- so clear in your mind? Simple question.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you -- you can probably see that it -- it does take me some time to remember stuff that I need time to answer your questions. I could not answer him immediately, but after a certain while I told him that I'd heard that he wasn't there, and then I told Mr. Petrusic all about the reasons that I was aware of for General Miletic not being around on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is back in September, end of September, how long was that certain while? How long did it take you before you told him the story? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during that same conversation. Maybe ten minutes. In any case, it didn't take me that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If this is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's the Prosecution's position that it's impossible. Nobody can go back 13 years in a manner of minutes and remember what somebody told them about whether or not someone was at a party. That just can't be done. Can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am telling you that I do remember. And not only that, I remember some other details. Some not as clearly, some clearly enough. This is about my birthday, which does not happen every day, does it. It's a very specific case. One's birthday is but once in a year. And those are the things that I can remember almost immediately and with clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to go back to page 5, line 10, and just read you what you said to us and just make sure about it. You said that: "We submitted regular reports when the war started, and sometime up to mid-1993 we submitted written reports, and as the time onwards reports were oral. We submitted reports to the deputy chief of the Main Staff at first, to the chief of the Main Staff, and later on to the operations department in the operations centre where General Miletic was at the time." So, Mr. Babic, is it correct that you first submitted reports to the deputy chief of the Main Staff, and then to the chief of the Main Staff, and then later on to the operations department?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the initial period written reports were submitted, and they were addressed to the Main Staff, but they probably ended up in the operations centre. After that, the deputy chief of the Main Staff ordered that verbal reports be made, and we made them to the Chief of Staff. And later still, reports were turned over to the operations centre where General Miletic was, and they were still verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a second. There seems to be some translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have him take off his earphones, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you understand some English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I -- I can clarify with him directly. What did you mean when you said deputy chief of Main Staff, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Deputy commander of the Main Staff and the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, which is the same person, and of course Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that clarify your concern? Thank you. Let's proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you said deputy -- did you say deputy chief the first time and you left out deputy commander, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the deputy commander and the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you -- but you did say deputy chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it really is not fair to the witness, because this is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't really hear the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's really a question of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, what he meant is one thing and what he said is another. So I think the question is quite fair. So let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, one more time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'll hear once again Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind for the witness to answer the question, but he never use these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure he'll say that now, but that was of course was the issue that I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. Ask the question and let's hear what the witness is going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, trying to ignore what you just heard Ms. Fauveau say, did you say "deputy Chief of Staff of the Main Staff" by mistake, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mistake. Let me clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Before you clarify, can you just tell us. So you did say deputy Chief of Staff and it's a mistake, and you want to explain your mistake; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Let me explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness start again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, if you could start again. The witness -- the interpreters missed the first part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deputy commander of the Main Staff and the chief of the Main Staff is one and the same person, General Milovanovic. His duty was transferred onto the units that were directly tied to the Main Staff, and among those units was also the Communications Regiment, i.e., the 67th Communications Regiment, my unit. Along the command line we were tied to him, and we reported to him orally. And as for the written reports, I have already explained previously how this was done. In the second half of that period that same person ordered us to send reports or hand over reports at the operations centre where General Miletic stayed or spent quite a lot of time because his office was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When General Milovanovic was in Belgrade and out of touch, who would you have given your reports to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Milovanovic was not available at the command post for whatever reason, we made our reports to General Miletic because he was the one replacing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes. Do you still have an objection, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If these question -- questions are to continue, maybe the Prosecutor can define the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought it was a hypothetical question. Do you have comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was going off at my earlier objection when we got into 1995, and I was assuming it was 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was one thing -- one way to call General Miletic when he was -- when he was replacing Milovanovic, was he the deputy Chief of Staff then?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't call him deputy Chief of Staff, because he did not hold that office, but in the absence of General Milovanovic he stood in for him as far as these issues were concerned. He was the senior officer to whom these reports were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you talked about two documents. One is P183. That's this 14 July -- if we could bring that one up, the 14th of July document by Tolimir asking for certain kinds of radios and communication. And you had some kind of problems with this. Did you ask or did the Defence offer to show you the original of that document?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see the original. I can see this one is a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me show you an original, and let me tell you that it came from a collection given to us by Republika Srpska authorities called the -- referred to as the Drina Corps collection, and it came in a packet with a cardboard thing on top. Sir, if you could just look at me for one second so I can show you this. Sorry, I've divided your attention. That's my fault. But let me show you. This came out of a packet of stuff from this pig collection that had this -- it says "telegram," and you can see what it says, and in it were a whole bunch of documents in the same size and looks very similar, and you can see the original ink -- sorry, I'll show you the original ink on another one. Now if you could just take a look at that one.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have listened to you carefully, and I followed the document, not the file you were showing me that I can. This is a bit of a different situation. However, even here the stamp and seal are missing of the station that received it and the encrypting officer who worked on it. We can't see whether this telegram was transmitted or received. This telegram, if received, then I accept that it normally doesn't have a signature; but if it was transmitted, then it should have a signature and a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, does this look like a typewriter to you or a teleprinter or something else based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Does this look like type from a typewriter, teleprinter, or something else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written on a teleprinter, RTL 100. That's how it's called. And that is the machine used in communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you can see up in the right-hand corner where it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, can you put the original on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, could you hand that to the usher. Thanks. And if we could -- and for the -- sir, if you look in the upper right-hand corner you can tell that's the original in ink; right? If you look at the actual document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the original ink for the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. And you can -- you can see that it says "sent" there; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "sent," "transmitted." However, every station had a stamp envisaged by establishment for that station, and that stamp has typed out various times and rubrics for which data had to be enter and a signature block. This is not the way it's done. It's not how things are done at teleprinter stations and stations for transmission and receipt of this sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'll help you out a little bit, sir. You wouldn't expect a received stamp on this because this was the document that was sent; right? If we just base on what is said on the document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was sent, then it should have a stamp and a signature in the lower part, the bottom left part. There should be a signature of the officer who drafted the document. At the stop we see command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, and the indication below is Assistant Commander Major-General Zdravko Tolimir, and the two don't match. If this officer indicated below is the one who drafted the document, he should have signed it, and the signature doesn't go without a stamp. There should be a stamp here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with you, there should be. And I can help you out a little bit by telling you that Danko Gojkovic -- have you heard of Danko Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he was a Coms guy for the Rogatica Brigade, and he's testified here and said he didn't have a stamp. Sometimes soldiers don't have everything they need; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, but in that case a written report cannot be submitted. It's not the regulation. The encryption teleprinter operator should not send, should not transmit an unverified, unauthorised document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think we can both agree that sometimes regulations get overlooked in war; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, here there are a number of elements, in fact two or three that are mutually contradicting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another one. You say that after this is sent, after it's encrypted and sent, General Tolimir should be waiting around the encryption room to sign the -- a copy like this? Is that right? Is that the regs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll come back to this outgoing telegram, a document that is to be transmitted. It has to be signed. It has to be transmit to the station. If it was General Tolimir signed here, he had to sign it. It could also be signed by somebody authorised by Tolimir, but in any case, it had to be signed. I agree with you if we assume there was no stamp, but I don't believe that at this level there was a station of cryptographic protection that did not have a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, whether you believe Mr. Gojkovic or not, you can certainly imagine that General Tolimir, on the 14th of July, the first day of a major assault on Zepa, may not want to be -- just hanging around the encryption machine so he can properly follow the regs and get it signed. You can imagine that might happen, can't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can imagine that, but in that case there would have been someone who would have signed on his behalf, because the soldier, the operator in the station would not otherwise know whether it was indeed ordered by General Tolimir or not. I have not seen this document before. This is the first time I'm seeing it. But from what I have learned, from what I was taught, documents have to be properly processed, and that implies all the elements I described. If we talk the signature of the ordering officer, if it's missing that can sometimes be explained by the circumstances, but everything is missing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you really think somebody would sign for General Tolimir if General Tolimir hadn't given them his specific authority? Isn't that why there's no signature on there? He sent this request. Somebody typed it up. Somebody sent it off to its address, and Tolimir was busy fighting the war; and nobody dared sign for it, and that's why that document is the way it is. Isn't that certainly possible?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. Why wouldn't it be possible? I'm not disputing that. I'm just saying that this is against the regulations. This is not a proper document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. And it's the position of the Prosecution that one of the reasons these documents still existed is because they're a little different than the main ones and they got missed when these things were looked for and cleaned out by people that would have done that. Do you know anything about culling through the archives of the VRS to take out documents that may be damaging?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No for several reasons. Through a combination of circumstances, just after the war, I changed position. I was no longer Chief of Staff. In the beginning of 1997, I assumed my duties in the communications organ of what was then the General Staff, and just after the war, in 1996, some other things were happening, and I did not eyewitness the destruction of archives or anything related to such destruction. I heard talk about the necessity to put order into the archives as envisaged by the rules governing archives and filing, certain deadlines for keeping material, and that is the sort of activity I performed in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you did hear about the archives and the need to get them ordered.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were they then?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. You mean the place where they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The archive of my unit, the regiment command, was kept within the unit, and the rest of the archives such as the archives of the Main Staff I had nothing to do with. I had no insight into that; I had no access, didn't know where it was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, your records are important records of the Main Staff archives, so I mean, they would have been archived with the other stuff; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then. In 1996, the archive of the regiment was in the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in 1996 this institution was here. It had indicted General Mladic. It had indicted President Karadzic and a few others. So any discussion about the archives, especially communications material, should have involved discussions about identifying material related to criminal charges, if for nothing else to show how innocent they were, or to destroy stuff that might -- or hide stuff that might show how they're guilty. So what did you hear about on those subjects?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the regiment was not involved in combat activities in relation to various actions that were executed. We only provided communications, as I described earlier, and to the best of my knowledge; which is extensive, there were no documents in the regiment archive that could be compromising -- that could be compromising to the commander of the Main Staff or the men indicted. In the war, the number of these documents that we kept was reduced. A lot less documents were produced than would have been in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. You can continue if you're answering my question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was about to say that there was no need within the regiment to destroy, as you put it, or hide any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would the regiment have kept, say, an order from General Mladic that was addressed to the regiment?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter P00046, and let me give you a hard copy of that. This is a document that came out of the Miletic's operations branch by the number 03-4, dated 21 July 1995. It's an order signed by General Mladic, and basically what it is is an order that, among other things, says that all the units that were participating in the Srebrenica operation should get some of the war booty. And on paragraph 6, it says: "The commission shall provide the following from war booty for the needs of the units that participated in combat: The 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, the 67th Communications Regiment, and the Sabotage Battalion. Ten top of the range colour TV sets in perfect working order, ten video recorders, ten freezers and ten washing machines. Make a record of these goods and hand them over to the relevant organs through the logistics organs." Did you guys get a television set out of Srebrenica or a freezer?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen this document before. I know nothing about this. And as for the goods listed in here, the Communications Regiment received nothing. At that time, the regiment was in a very bad situation as regards its accommodation and living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So -- and a more important question would be: So was General Mladic wrong when he concluded in this paragraph that the 67th Communication Regiment participated in the combat?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure he was wrong, because the Communication Regiment did not participate in the combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 2D00142. I've got a copy of this. It's a bad photocopy, so it may be easier to read on the screen if they blow it up for you a bit, but this is a 17 July order, again out of the Operations and Training Administration, according to the number. It's again signed by Ratko Mladic, and this one is actually addressed to the 67th Communications Regiment under "Very urgent," and it says: "As of 17 July," on paragraph 3, "the forces of the 1st Bratunac Brigade, the 1st Milici Brigade, the 67th," that's the Communications Regiment, "will comb the territory in the zone of Bratunac ..." and then it talks about the commands. So clearly the 67th Protection Regiment had guys with guns that could do this kind of sweep operation; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 67th Regiment had young soldiers in training, signalsmen who had their own personal weapons. I mean rifles, automatic rifles. I've never seen this document before. This is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go back --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to your memory. Go back to the fall of Srebrenica. I'm sure you've had a lot of time to think about this, and a lot of time to think about your testimony, and a lot of time to think about those events. Did your unit have a combat unit? You've already told us about the duty to protect Crna Rijeka. Did your guys had a combat unit that took part in this -- this important operation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Communication Regiment did not have any involvement in the operation around Srebrenica. Its only form of participation was stepping up security of the part of the command post providing security for the units which were on a stand-by in case of attack, the Main Staff, the communications service, and the communications also -- the Communications Regiment also boosted measures in order to prevent leaks of information via communications means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir. Let me -- this will be my last question. Maybe it will jog your memory. But 17 July is about five days after the 12th of July when the VRS and MUP forces entered in Potocari and took Srebrenica and took the whole enclave. I'm sure you'll remember that, a couple of days, the 12th and the 13th thousands of Muslims were shipped out towards Kladanj. And you may remember on the 16th of July the Muslims that were going towards Zvornik got into a very bloody battle with the Zvornik Brigade and others. And on the 17th of July, this Court has heard testimony about the army and the MUP were involved in a sweep operation in the area described by this particular order, and they've heard that 100-plus Muslims were captured in that sweep order; and I can tell you those Muslims have never been seen since, and it's the position of the Prosecutor that they were summarily executed. And we've got a document that says your unit is involved in that sweep operation. So put all of that in your head. Does that jog your memory about the involvement of your unit in this horrendous crime?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have just one question about Exhibit number P46, the previous document that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Babic, who was this order addressed to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was addressed to the command of the Drina Corps, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Babic, that concludes your testimony, and on behalf of the Tribunal, I'd like to thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope I've been of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, documents. Do you have any documents to tender, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart tells me that 2D00142, the 17 July -- it's hard for me to imagine that's not in evidence. Maybe another version of it is, but that should -- that should go. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is P37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's under P927, so we don't need to worry about that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not 37?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, P927 was that 17 July document that was probably -- that replaces 2D00142. It just went in years ago, and I'm sure we didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just am looking at P37, which seems to be similar to me. Well, that can be sorted out later on either way. I take it that we have two identical documents. That said, okay. Very well. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kralj. If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you give us your name and surname, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Slavko Kralj.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you give us your educational background and what schools you have completed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I graduated from a school for non-commissioned officers in Banja Luka in 1967, and then I passed my exam to become a commissioned officer and receive my commission five years later. I also passed exams to become a major. I also continued education for officers in charge of command and staff duties at the brigade level. I also completed a training course for battalion commanders. I also have a degree in English from a training course in Belgrade. I completed many training courses, including a training course for officers who were sent as members of peacekeeping missions of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What were your duties before the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Throughout my military career I was a tank commander, a tank platoon commander, the commander of an independent tank unit, a desk officer for training at the military school in Banja Luka further on. I was an observer, a United Nations observer as a member of UNIMOG mission in 1989, from February to February, on the board are between Iraq and Iran. That was from 1989 to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where were you in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I was a member of the 1st Krajina Corps, and I served as a communications officer. Rather, a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When did you join the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Together with the rest of the officers by a decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just before joining the army of the Republika Srpska, could you tell us where you were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I was a desk officer in the school centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You told us that you had been liaison officer in the 1st Corps of the Krajina. What other posts did you have in the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand your question. What time? What period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In May 1992, you were liaison officer of the 1st Corps of the Krajina. Did you -- were you in these posts during the whole war, or did you have other missions, other assignments?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In the 1st Krajina Corps, I stayed up until the beginning of November 1994, and then I was reassign to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska as an interpreter for English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you belonged to the staff of the Republika Srpska, in what particular organ were you serving?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This was the department for communication with international military representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to start with your assignments in the 1st Krajina Corps. Who was your director, supervisor, in the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Your Honours, my superior in the 1st Krajina Corps was Colonel Gojko Vujnovic. He was the chief of the department for civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you repeat the name of the unit of which Colonel Vujnovic was the chief, the department?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This was the newly establish organ in the 1st Corps, and its title was the department for civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you describe for us your tasks and assignments in the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: My task was primarily to translate documents that arrived in the corps that were in English. I also maintained contacts with foreign military representatives and international organisations. That was my task as a liaison officer. In order to organise contacts and meetings between the corps commander and the aforementioned persons, I had to perform all of my tasks that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D785, please. It's an order from the Main Staff of the 6th of August, 1993, which was sent to all the corps of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you look at item 2 of this order.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
